title: Investigating Memory in RL with POPGym Arcade
claim: A suite of paired fully and partially observable environments, plus a memory-analysis tool, lets us study how agents use memory.
layout: 2 stacked parts: environment twin grid on top, recurrent diagram with overlaid plot below
description: The figure has two parts. The top is a dark-titled panel, "MDP/POMDP Twins", containing a 2x5 grid of retro pixel-art game screenshots: Cartpole, Skittles, Breakout, Minesweeper and Tetris. The top row shows the fully observable version of each game. The bottom row shows the partially observable twin, with information removed (for example, no cartpole, hidden mines and fewer blocks). Below the panel is a plot with axes. Four light-blue bars with dots mark memory access at observations o1 to o4, and an orange curve passes through the dots. A blue integral of a policy gradient norm and an orange expectation formula label the plot. Underneath, a chain of green recurrent boxes f takes inputs o1 to o4 and passes hidden states h0 to h3. The last box outputs the state estimate ŝ4 into a lavender policy box π(a4|ŝ4).
caption: A few of our MDP/POMDP twins, enabling counterfactual studies of memory. We also provide memory analysis tools, such as the recall density function (\textbf{orange}), which aggregates memory accesses (\textbf{blue}) over trajectories to understand how agents use memory ($h$).
abstract: How should we analyze memory in deep RL? We introduce tools for analyzing policies under partial observability and revealing how agents use memory to make decisions. To utilize these tools, we present POPGym Arcade, a collection of Atari-inspired, hardware-accelerated environments sharing a single observation and action space. Each environment provides fully and partially observable variants, enabling counterfactual studies on observability. We find that controlled studies are necessary for fair comparisons and identify a pathology where value functions smear credit over irrelevant history. Using this pathology, we demonstrate how out-of-distribution scenarios can contaminate memory, perturbing the policy far into the future.
